Listen to this article Share Zimbabwean investors have until Wednesday, October 21, to apply for shares in Aliko Dangote’s refinery, as the Nigerian billionaire’s record initial public offering opens its doors to more investors across Africa. The Financial Securities Exchange (FINSEC) extended the local application window for depositary receipts in Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals from October 9 to October 21, The Herald reported. The offer opened on September 29, giving Zimbabwean investors more time to participate in the $1.6 billion share sale. The extension follows a decision by Nigeria’s Securities and Exchange Commission to move the main offer’s closing date from October 13 to October 27. FINSEC’s deadline comes earlier to allow time for application checks, exchange control documentation, regulatory approvals, and transferring subscriptions to Nigeria. Read also: Dangote Refinery IPO reaches Zimbabwe, as Nigerian Lawmakers extend 2025 budget for 4th time & Investors avoid mining sector over insecurity David Bird, chief executive of the refinery, welcomed the extension, saying it would help the company attract investors from across the continent. “We welcome the SEC’s approval of the extension,” he said. The indicative price is 40 cents per depositary receipt, although the final amount may change with exchange rate movements. FINSEC said the final offer price would determine how many receipts each investor receives, and any unused balance could be refunded. Applications must include a completed form and an exchange control declaration. Investors who fail to submit the required documents risk having their money returned. How Zimbabweans can participate Zimbabwean investors are participating through a Southern African depositary receipt programme anchored in Botswana. Access Bank Botswana plans to issue up to $500 million worth of receipts, with trading expected to begin on December 14. The minimum investment for Zimbabwean applicants is $100. Applications can be made through the C-TRADE platform and EcoCash, BusinessDay reported. Depositary receipts allow investors to gain exposure to shares in a company through a local market arrangement, rather than purchasing and holding the underlying shares directly through the foreign exchange where the company is listed. Zimbabwe is among several African markets being opened to the offer as Dangote seeks to widen participation beyond Nigeria. Investors in Kenya have been cleared to buy global depositary receipts, while access in Uganda and Ethiopia is restricted to professional and wealthy investors. Rwanda’s Capital Markets Authority said in September that it was working on arrangements to enable local investors to participate. The Egyptian Exchange is also in talks with Dangote Group over a possible Egyptian depositary receipt programme. Read also: Who was Wicknell Chivayo, the Zimbabwean billionaire killed in a helicopter crash The refinery said on Sunday that subscriptions had come from more than 90 countries, including 51 of Africa’s 54 nations, underscoring its efforts to attract capital from across the continent. Record share sale to fund expansion Dangote Petroleum Refinery is offering 4.1 billion shares at N525 each, targeting proceeds of about N2.15 trillion, or $1.6 billion. The offer is the largest initial public offering in Nigeria’s history. The proceeds are expected to support plans to double the refinery’s capacity to 1.4 million barrels per day and expand its fuel storage and distribution operations. The company reported a net profit of $4.7 billion for the nine months to September 30, on revenue of $22.5 billion. The figures highlight the scale of the business as it seeks investment to finance further expansion. At that valuation, Dangote’s stake in the refinery would be worth about $55 billion. The cross-border offer also provides a test of whether African capital markets can make it easier for investors in different countries to finance major businesses on the continent. For Zimbabwean investors, the immediate priority is meeting the October 21 deadline, while the broader success of the offer will depend on investor demand and the arrangements used to connect national markets.
